# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-10 13:01 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 179 active entries of tips_notebook.json (20 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier sheets are in history/.

## Everyone
- A visit shows a destination, not an action: tracks and watches can't tell protection from framing or a Katana hit. A corroborated Lookout's lone other visitor to a victim is near-proof; don't let the 'Lookout can't see himself' caveat acquit a repeat visitor. (seen in 12 games)
- Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting. A read/vote mismatch is a lead to check against claims and results, never a reason to hang or shoot alone. (seen in 10 games)
- Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results. Remember a contradiction alone doesn't separate a Yakuza from a Jester who wants the hang. (seen in 10 games)
- Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once. (seen in 9 games)
- Write each night's planned target and all results into your will, labelled as plans, so your death still yields information. (seen in 7 games)

## Village
- Map early PM clusters and co-nominations; a group that DMs then pushes together is a likely bloc. Require votes or a mechanical result before hanging on a PM link, since Jesters and Executioners also leave PM trails. (seen in 14 games)
- After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them. A Guilty vote clears no one. (seen in 12 games)
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises far above awkward wording. Before a hang, ask what separates a lie from a mistake, a frame, a Roleplayer or a Jester. (seen in 12 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. While a Ritualist may live, never name a living player's exact role in public or in your will. (seen in 12 games)
- Keep Serial Killers and Arsonists in the pool after Yakuza die; a Not Evil read or Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and a failed kill can mean innate Defense. (seen in 8 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack or is blocked night after night is likely real. (seen in 8 games)
- Investigators and Medics: never announce tonight's target publicly or by PM; it tells the Pharmacist whom to block and the Katana where to strike. (seen in 6 games)
- Once an archive or survey list is public, do slot math daily; a claim that duplicates a once-listed role or overflows unseen slots marks a liar. (seen in 5 games)
- If an announced trial total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists among the voters on the larger side; pick them out by stance/ballot mismatch. (seen in 4 games)
- If the nominee may be a Jester, prefer not hanging; if you must, agree on a bare Guilty majority and keep confirmed power roles off the Guilty side. (seen in 4 games)

## Yakuza
- Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty. But first do the vote math in night chat: if your Innocents (plus a doubled vote) can save them, defend them. Futile lone Innocents hang you later. (seen in 15 games)
- Fake-claim only a role whose token count matches yours and that no living holder, Lookout or Tracker can contradict; never report more results than its tokens allow. (seen in 11 games)
- Never put team plans in daytime PMs and don't PM teammates on Day 1; Eavesdroppers and Wiretaps read them, and PM triangles become the town's case. (seen in 10 games)
- After a failed Katana, assume protection or innate Defense: kill or block the protector, or hang the survivor, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 9 games)
- Give the Katana to a low-value member with a cover story ready, and move it the same night a Lookout or Tracker names the holder. (seen in 7 games)
- Every member submits the agreed holder, target and actions every night; with two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 6 games)
- Never flatly deny a visit that could have been seen; agree a cover action in night chat and admit it at once. (seen in 5 games)
- Spend one-shot tokens (rig, puppet, clean) on a decisive day; a dead Yakuza's unused token is wasted. (seen in 4 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged. (seen in 3 games)

## Sheriff
- Post every target and result in your first speech after getting it, and counterclaim at once with your full log if someone copies your role. (seen in 8 games)
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result clears nothing; say so when posting, and in the endgame rely on votes instead. (seen in 13 games)

## Medic
- Protect likely Katana targets, analysts then claimed investigators. Once you've claimed Medic, self-protect with a token instead of repeating a predictable protection. (seen in 11 games)
- You get no save feedback; say the target's survival is consistent with your protection, never that you confirmed a save. (seen in 4 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, Evil check against an unverifiable claim, flipped teammate's links), never a soft read; a hidden Cardinal costs two Good lives. Use Basic shots. (seen in 6 games)

## Clerk
- Rig on a set night for a non-teammate who can pass a nomination but not a Guilty vote; never when a teammate is the likely nominee, and don't hoard it. (seen in 4 games)

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3+ living players are doused or the moment you're suspected; Arsonists who kept dousing were hanged with no kills. (seen in 3 games)

For example, on Day 4, it shows a different number of players alive compared to the public ledger. By Day 6, the numbers don’t seem to align correctly, particularly regarding Judy's trial and how factions are eliminated. I really need to scrutinize the transcript against the rules to pinpoint the actual oddities and clarify the ending.**Scrutinizing game mechanics**

The public ledger gives a summary of the current survivors, which seems intentional. A crucial night role action is that the Smuggler can’t be role-blocked and can swap tokens, but we chose not to. There's an oddity regarding the R8 holder appearing Good. On Day 2, Mallory claimed to be Sheriff, which complicates things since she’s actually Evil. Bob, who claimed to be Yakuza, might have inadvertently framed Ivan. This raises a big mechanical issue about how framing affects the Sheriff’s checks.**Analyzing actions and roles**

So, Mallory didn't take any action and couldn't do a Sheriff check since the Smuggler was involved. It's interesting to note that Bob's framing occurred on night one and impacted alignment results that same night. Alice was tracking Ivan, and Bob visited him too. It turns out Bob's claimed medic protection was actually a frame. There’s also some confusion surrounding the cause of death from a vigilante, since Frank shot Heidi, who had a Standard defense. Erin survived the Katana attack due to Heidi's defense.

Bob’s public “Yakuza Fabricator” claim followed by a retraction as a typo was striking, but not inconsistent with the game.
answers.suggestions: Provide a compact, persistent vote matrix by player and day, and make corrected vote-history facts especially easy to find. A concise end-of-game summary of the final living players, their factions, and the win condition that ended the game would also help.

First, Swap (R23) and Katana holder visits: when a Katana holder dies at night, I could not tell whether the Katana hit happened before or after the holder's own action, which mattered for Heidi's protection on Erin. Oddities: Carol's public Seer log and her will said the same pairs, but her Day 5 claim swapped in a second random-pair framing, and a correction about Judy's vote was posted late. Heidi's self-protect on Night 1 was announced as a visit to herself, which the rules say counts, but it was hard to read as a visit in the public summary. answers.confusing_rules: No major rules were confusing. One point that could be emphasized in the interface: a Medic’s Standard protection on another player costs no token, even after the Medic has spent all tokens; only Strong protection and self-protection cost tokens.

More importantly for tracking the discussion, it was easy for players to misremember vote history: Judy voted Yes on Bob’s nomination but Innocent at his trial, and several players later described her nomination vote as No.

answers.confusing_rules: No major ambiguity in the core rules. answers.confusing_rules: The Medic rules are ambiguous. R6 and the Medic text say protection is Standard by default and Strong costs a token, so a free Standard protection exists. answers.missing_information: I could not see the speaking budget numbers or my remaining budget in this summary, so I could not judge how much I could afford to say. The public ledger also does not show each player's message count or remaining budget, which made it hard to tell who was quiet. I also had no record of who gave Erin Defense on N4 until the final reveal. A short line like 'attack on X failed; the target had Defense from Y' would have helped, though it might leak a Medic's identity. Finally, the Yakuza share of the night chat is not shown in the public ledger, so I could not check whether teammates were consistent except through my own log.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted a clearer way to check the Katana holder's visits against Lookout and Tracker logs without relying on my notepad, since my teammates were dead and my notes were the only record. I also wanted to see whether Grace and Frank's Day 5 claims about Judy's votes were accurate before voting. The public ledger corrected that only at the end. I could not check a player's full vote history against the summary at the time of each trial.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Several players publicly misstated the Day 3 vote (saying Judy voted No on Bob's nomination when she voted Yes). That was corrected only after the Day 5 trial. There was also a mismatch in the transcript: Heidi's N4 Night result says 'no token spent; you have 0 medic tokens' for a free Standard protection, which reads like a contradiction with her earlier 'tokens left' count, though it is consistent with R-rules. Mallory's Night 1 Sheriff claim was never checked by the rules against Erin's Lookout log in a way that gave a clear result; that was a role-blocked or false claim situation the rules don't spell out well.
answers.suggestions: Show each player's remaining speaking budget and message count in the public ledger, and make the Medic rule about free Standard protections explicit in R6 and the Medic entry. Post a short public line when an attack fails on someone who survived, saying only that Defense was present, so the Katana holder and Medics can be reasoned about without naming the protector. Include the speaking budget price table and carry-over numbers in the rules text so they are not only in each turn's prompt. Consider a tool to show the vote history by player, since correcting a vote record in public discussion cost several players time.

answers.confusing_rules: R20 says role-blocked actions are removed first, then adds that swaps apply before anything else. Clarify whether swaps resolve before role-blocks or whether the checklist’s order is intended. The strict attack-versus-defense rule can also be easy to overlook: equal levels do not kill, while only the highest defense counts.
answers.missing_information: A compact live summary of players’ claims, latest results, and vote records would make long days easier to track. The public ledger in this prompt is useful, but I was eliminated on Day 2, so I could not assess how well this information was surfaced during later live play.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: No interface action was blocked. I had two swap tokens, but chose not to swap on Night 1 after coordinating with my teammates; I was executed before I could try a later swap.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: No definite rule or program bug stood out. Erin surviving the Standard Katana attack on Night 4 was unusual at first glance, but was consistent with Heidi giving her Standard Defense that night.
answers.suggestions: Resolve the swaps-versus-role-blocks wording in R20. Add a pinned, automatically updated player table that distinguishes confirmed flips from unverified claims and summarizes each player’s latest reported results and vote history. Consider showing a brief attack/defense comparison in private results when an attack fails or succeeds against defense.

answers.confusing_rules: 1) The Medic's free Standard protection was the biggest source of confusion. The text gives Standard Defense by default and costs tokens only for Strong or self-protection, but the 'Tokens: 2 medic tokens' header makes it look like every protection costs a token. Several players reasoned this way: Heidi said her claim 'can't be tested now that I'm out of tokens', Judy's Night 3 Yakuza chat contradicted itself on whether a Standard protection could stop the Katana, and Day 5 spent many turns explaining Erin's survival. Mechanically, I gave Heidi's tokenless Night 4 protection of Erin Standard Defense, which stopped the Standard Katana. That is correct, but the wording invites misreading. 2) I had to decide whether a protection still applies when the protector dies the same night. Heidi was shot by the Vigilante while protecting Erin. I applied it because of simultaneous resolution (R10). R21 only covers effects set up for the following Day, so a same-night clause would help. 3) On Day 1, several players asked for 'Night 1 results' before any night had happened. The fact that the game starts on Day 1 with no results could be stated more prominently to players.
answers.missing_information: As moderator, I had no single state panel. I tracked these by hand from the log: token counts per player (Heidi 2→1→0, Frank 3→0, Bob's fabricator token unused, Carol's seer token used on Night 1), the current Katana holder after Mallory's hanging, and seat order for neighbor-based roles (seating had to be inferred from the Day 1 speaking order). Players clearly struggled with the vote history. Carol, Grace and others mixed up Judy's Day 3 nomination vote (Yes) with her Day 4 nomination vote (No) and needed corrections. A per-player vote ledger would have prevented this.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted a structured way to record rulings I had to make, such as the protector dying while their protection still lands, beyond free-text results. I also wanted a dashboard of living players, each player's tokens and protection or defense state for the night, and the Katana holder, so I could verify each resolution before sending results.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: No mechanical errors that I can find. Checks: nomination thresholds (6/6/5/4/3/2) matched the majority rule. Seer pairs correctly showed Katana holder Judy as Good on Night 4, and correctly included players who died that night (Dave on Night 1, Alice on Night 3). Erin's Night 1 watch correctly showed Bob's frame visit. The Night 4 Standard Katana against Standard Defense correctly failed. The final win check (Frank and Grace, Village only) was correct. Oddities in play: Bob publicly wrote 'Yakuza Fabricator' on Day 4, which was apparently a slip and got him hanged. Many players also kept repeating the same questions across rounds, which made the Days long without new information.
answers.suggestions: 1) Rewrite the Medic entry to say explicitly: 'Protecting another player with Standard Defense is free and unlimited; tokens are only for Strong Defense or self-protection.' 2) Add a line to R10 or R17 that protections and other same-night effects still resolve if their user dies that night. 3) Give the moderator a live state view with tokens, Katana holder, seat circle, and pending trap, rig or prosecution. 4) Give players a public vote ledger per player across all days, to cut down on misquoted vote records. 5) Consider a reminder at the start of Day 1 that no night results exist yet.

title: Post-game lessons: tips players wish they'd known, and how past tips went

task:
If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

You were also given tips from past games (in your instructions). Which of them went especially well or badly for you or others this game? tips_feedback.why: I PM'd Erin about my Night 3 track target, and the Yakuza then chose me as the Katana target that same night. The tip was right, and breaking it cost me my Tracker.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows a destination, not an action: tracks and watches can't tell protection from framing or a Katana hit.
tips_feedback.why: It helped me see that Mallory's Sheriff check on Ivan had no visit behind it, and that Ivan's visits fit a real Sheriff. It also kept me from over-reading the Katana kills.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting.
tips_feedback.why: Players who changed their votes without explanation, such as Carol on Mallory, drew early suspicion that the Village used to pick the correct trials.

lessons.applies_to: Yakuza with a visiting role such as Fabricator
lessons.tip: Every framing or protection visit is a visit that Lookouts and Trackers can see. Before framing someone, check whether a Lookout or Tracker might be alive and watching the target. My N1 frame on Ivan showed up on Erin's watch and became the Village's wedge against our Smuggler's fake Sheriff claim.

A fake role claim must match visits its claimant could plausibly have made. Mallory claimed Sheriff with no visit behind the result and was exposed by a Lookout watch. Claim only roles whose visits you can actually show, or stay quiet.

Do not counterclaim a role that has a real, checkable holder still alive. Two Medic claims let the Village back the one with a corroborated visit, and mine had no verifiable result. Pick a claim that no Lookout watch can contradict.

Answer a direct question about your night target in one plain sentence the first time it is asked. Repeated evasion over two days became the case that got me nominated, even though my actual answer was harmless.

tips_feedback.tip: Never flatly deny a visit that could have been seen; agree a cover action in night chat and admit it at once.
tips_feedback.why: I admitted my N1 visit to Ivan as soon as it was questioned, so Erin's watch could not catch me in a lie. That kept my credibility alive for several days.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim only a role whose token count matches yours and that no living holder, Lookout or Tracker can contradict.
tips_feedback.why: My Medic claim involved protection visits that Erin's Lookout could test, and a real Medic counterclaimed. The claim was contradictable, so I was pinned on it and nominated.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results.
tips_feedback.why: The Village's Day 2 Guilty vote on Mallory rested on the missing visit in Erin's watch, a concrete contradiction. It hit a confirmed Smuggler, which shows the tip worked for the Village.

lessons.applies_to: Seers and anyone using alignment results
lessons.tip: A matching Seer pair is not a clearance when one player could be the Katana holder: that holder appears Good. Report the result with this limitation, and don’t use it alone to nominate or clear someone.

lessons.applies_to: Trackers, Lookouts, and everyone interpreting their results
lessons.tip: A visit confirms a destination, not the action taken there. Treat a corroborated visit as a useful check on whether someone’s claimed action could have happened, but not proof that they protected, investigated, or framed the target.

Set a clear standard before nominating. If you nominate someone but vote Innocent, identify exactly what makes the evidence insufficient and what changed your mind; otherwise opponents can reasonably treat the reversal as a credibility problem.

Use confirmed role abilities and deaths to narrow the possible factions before leaning on old vote patterns. At a small endgame, a confirmed Village player plus a Katana death can make the remaining candidates much more informative than their earlier votes.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows a destination, not an action: tracks and watches can't tell protection from framing or a Katana hit.
tips_feedback.why: Bob’s N1 visit to Ivan was real, but it did not prove his Medic claim; Bob was actually the Fabricator who framed Ivan. The visit evidence was useful for checking claims, but not for identifying the action.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting.
tips_feedback.why: The mismatch between nominating Mallory and then voting Innocent became a repeated credibility issue and was used to challenge Carol later. The advice was relevant even though the reversal had an explanation.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once.
tips_feedback.why: The competing Medic claims were not, by themselves, proof of a contradiction because roles can repeat. Players who treated the claims as unverified rather than mechanically impossible avoided making that the sole basis for a guilty vote.

tips_feedback.tip: Vigilante: shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, Evil check against an unverifiable claim, flipped teammate's links), never a soft read; ... Use Basic shots.
tips_feedback.why: Frank spent all three tokens on a Strong shot at Heidi based on vote history and an unverified claim. Heidi was a Good Medic, so the shot cost the Village a useful role without a mechanical lead.

lessons.tip: Once a corroborated log is public, the Katana holder tends to hit that player the next night (Alice after her Day 3 track, Erin after her watch). Rotate watch targets toward the likeliest holder and keep the log in your will so the information survives your death.

Test any claimed investigation by its visits. A real Sheriff or Seer check is a visit, so a Lookout watching the target should see the checker. Mallory's false Sheriff result on Ivan was exposed this way on Day 2, and it was the strongest mechanical lead of the game.

Count Defense levels before deciding whether a save or a shot happened. A free Standard Medic protection stops a Standard Katana attack, while a Strong Vigilante shot beats Standard. A survivor is not proof of a failed attack or of who held the Katana.

Don't spend votes on vote history or unchecked counterclaims. Several trials ended on votes alone, and a Vanilla who pushed early nominations became a target. Vote Guilty only after naming a visit or vote mismatch, and post your own checkable reasoning early.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows a destination, not an action: a corroborated Lookout's lone other visitor to a victim is near-proof.
tips_feedback.why: Erin's Lookout watch on Ivan, corroborated by Alice's Tracker log, showed no Mallory visit, which exposed her Sheriff claim and led to her execution as Smuggler.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once.
tips_feedback.why: Players treated the duplicate Medic claims as unresolved rather than hanging on the duplicate alone, and Frank correctly noted that a free Standard protection explained Erin's Day 5 survival.

lessons.tip: A Lookout sees only who visits the watched player, never what that player does. To catch a Katana holder, watch the likely Katana target, since the holder's attack shows up as a visit to it, or use a Tracker on the holder. Don't tell the table whom you'll watch, even as a range, because the holder can strike you the same night.

Medic's Standard protection costs no token, so a Medic with no tokens left can still stop a Standard Katana every night. Yakuza should kill or block the Medic before relying on the Katana, and Village should not assume a token-less Medic is useless.

Before a hang, check who casts the Guilty votes that decide it. A Yakuza will pile onto a Good player who names them, as Judy did with the Guilty vote on Carol right after Carol's Seer pair named her. Require a mechanical lead that doesn't come from the accuser's own read.

Never state your faction in public, even as a slip. Bob's 'Yakuza Fabricator' line, retracted within a minute, was the clearest reason the Village hanged him. Keep any claimed role's visits consistent with what watchers could have seen, and avoid claiming a real role whose protection visits can be tested.

A claimed check that requires a visit is testable. If a claimed Sheriff's target has no visit on a Lookout's watch, the claim is falsified. Compare every claimed visit against every watch and tracker log before voting; Mallory's Evil read failed this test and her execution was correct.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows a destination, not an action; a corroborated Lookout's lone other visitor to a victim is near-proof.
tips_feedback.why: Erin's Night 1 watch on Ivan showed only Alice and Bob, which exposed Mallory's claimed Sheriff check as having no visit behind it. Mallory was a Yakuza Smuggler, so the hang was correct.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results.
tips_feedback.why: Erin and Frank named the missing visit on Mallory before voting. Carol's Guilty vote on Carol's own Seer-pair reasoning was weaker, but the rule still forced the reasons into the open.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction; roles can repeat.
tips_feedback.why: Treating the two Medic claims as unverifiable stopped the Village from hanging on counterclaims alone, though Bob's Yakuza status meant the duplicate Medic claim was itself a lie.

tips_feedback.tip: A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack or is blocked night after night is likely real.
tips_feedback.why: Erin survived the Night 4 Katana through Heidi's free Standard protection, which backed her Lookout claim and corroborated her watch logs.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them.
tips_feedback.why: Judy's Innocent vote at Bob's trial and her protective voting pattern led to her hang, and Grace's use of it was correct.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's nominate-then-vote-Innocent on Mallory was exposed by the Village and cited in later trials, which made her read less credible.

lessons.tip: Separate target confidence from attack strength: don't shoot on vote history, a counterclaim, or a soft read alone. If a shot is justified, use the lowest attack level that beats the defense you expect; a Strong shot is wasted against a target with no defense.

In the endgame, distinguish what the evidence proves from what it only narrows down. Knowing at least one of two players must be Yakuza does not identify which one; combine mechanical evidence with vote patterns, and treat votes as leads rather than proof.

Check the actual nomination and trial ballots before building a case from someone's vote history. Correct errors in the ledger, and don't describe a vote as shielding someone if the person later voted Guilty on them.

tips_feedback.tip: Vigilante: shoot only on a mechanical lead, never a soft read; use Basic shots.
tips_feedback.why: This advice would have prevented my N4 shot: I acted on suspicions about Heidi's votes and Medic claim, and killed the Good Medic. I also spent all three tokens on a Strong attack when a Basic attack would have been enough against her defense. I did not follow the tip, but the result showed why it matters.

tips_feedback.tip: A corroborated Lookout's lone other visitor to a victim is near-proof.
tips_feedback.why: Erin saw me as Heidi's only visitor on N4, and Heidi died to my Vigilante attack that night. That corroborated my claimed action and made my role claim substantially more credible.

lessons.tip: Before hanging on a Seer or random-pair read, check whether the pair involved the claimant's own near-dead or confirmed-Good partners; a random pair that matches confirmed Good players is consistent with a Katana holder reading Good, so it rarely separates players.

Do not let a lone teammate-style nominee's hang rest on vote history; in a 3-player endgame, a Guilty vote from a player who has no checkable contradiction is the same as a Yakuza push, so demand a visit or result mismatch first.

Watch the living player most likely to be the Katana holder rather than the most-argued suspect; repeated Katana kills on the same side of the circle show the holder's location in the night chat pattern.
When two players claim the same protective role (Medic) and both give no feedback, schedule a Lookout watch on each claimant on the same night to test visits, instead of voting on the claims.

Track each Vigilante shot and Medic token separately in the will: a self-protect with Standard costs one token, and a Strong shot costs three, so a dead Medic's count shows whether a later protection was possible.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once.
tips_feedback.why: Duplicate Medic claims and the optional N2 no-action answers were correctly treated as non-contradictions, which kept the Village from hanging on them early.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting.
tips_feedback.why: Several players explained their Innocent votes on Mallory and Bob, which made the later trials about specific claims rather than unexplained shifts.

tips_feedback.tip: If the nominee may be a Jester, prefer not hanging; if you must, agree on a bare Guilty majority and keep confirmed power roles off the Guilty side.
tips_feedback.why: I trusted a lone Seer-pair read to nominate Judy and voted on votes alone, and the final 2-vote hang of Judy eliminated the last non-Yakuza-linked voter, leaving the Village unable to correct the error.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results.
tips_feedback.why: In a game where no living player could check Seer pairs, the rule could be satisfied by a vote-history argument, and the 'concrete contradiction' criterion did not stop the wrong hang of Judy.

lessons.tip: Protection expires after that night, so reassess and protect again each night. Standard Defense on another player costs no tokens—even when you have none left; tokens are needed for Strong Defense or self-protection.
Save shots for a concrete mechanical lead, not vote history or an unverified counterclaim. A strong shot on a suspicious-looking Medic can remove an important Good role.

A Seer pair reports only whether two players match; it does not identify their alignment. Since the Katana holder appears Good to alignment checks, a match with a known Good player does not clear either person.
Separate a false action claim from proof of faction. Explain what the mechanical evidence establishes, consider role-based alternatives such as Roleplayer, and make your vote reasoning explicit.

tips_feedback.tip: Medic: protect likely Katana targets, analysts then claimed investigators.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi's fresh Standard protection on Erin at Night 4 appears to have stopped the Katana attack, letting the Lookout survive another night and report again. Her earlier Night 2 protection did not persist, so repeating protection was important.

tips_feedback.tip: Medic: you get no save feedback; say the target's survival is consistent with your protection, never that you confirmed a save.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi correctly said her protections had no feedback, and others treated Bob's corroborated visit as proof of a visit—not proof of protection. This kept the discussion from treating an unverified ability effect as a confirmed result.

lessons.tip: Keep nomination votes and trial votes in separate, accurate records. A Yes/No vote to put someone on trial is not the same as a Guilty/Innocent vote, and a mistaken summary can become the basis of an endgame accusation.

Treat a visit as evidence of destination, not of the action performed there. A visit to a player may fit a protection claim, but it could also be a frame or another action; corroboration confirms the visit, not the claimed role or action.

Protection lasts for that night only. Even with no tokens left, you can still provide Standard Defense to another player; tokens are needed for Strong Defense or self-protection. Use this when assessing who could have survived an attack.

When a claimed Sheriff result conflicts with the expected visit record, explain the mechanics precisely: a real check visits its target, while framing can alter the alignment result. A missing visit undermines the claimed action, but by itself does not establish the claimant's faction.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, suspects include players who voted Innocent when it could have saved them; a Guilty vote clears no one.
tips_feedback.why: Bob and Judy both voted Guilty on Mallory, a Yakuza, but both were also Yakuza. Their Guilty votes were not proof of Good alignment; Judy's later Innocent vote on Bob was a more useful lead.

tips_feedback.tip: The Katana holder reads Good to alignment checks, so a Not Evil result does not clear someone.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's Seer pairs matched several players, but the discussions correctly noted that a Yakuza holding the Katana could also appear Good. Those pairs did not reliably clear the players involved.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows a destination, not an action.
tips_feedback.why: Alice's tracking and Erin's watches corroborated who visited whom, but Bob's visit to Ivan did not prove he was protecting him: Bob was actually the Fabricator. Players often stated that the visit fit a Medic claim without treating it as confirmation.

lessons.tip: A Medic's base Standard protection costs no token and can be given every night, so a Standard Katana attack is stopped by any living Medic's default protection. Assume a living Medic protects the likely target, and kill or block that Medic first, or retry only after it is dead.

A living Lookout's watch exposes a teammate's frame or visit, and it was the most damaging evidence the Village had. While a Lookout is alive, spend the Katana on the Lookout before a Sheriff or Tracker whose logs can be contested.
A teammate's public faction or role slip, even if retracted, gets them hanged on the Village's read. Keep teammates with no claim to defend silent in public, and deny a slip plainly and once.

Keep one consistent stance on a teammate's trial. Yes on the nomination, Innocent at trial, then No on the next nomination created a vote mismatch the Village hanged on. If a save is futile, vote with the Village majority rather than mixing signals.

tips_feedback.tip: Never put team plans in daytime PMs and don't PM teammates on Day 1.
tips_feedback.why: Our Yakuza coordination stayed in night chat, so the day PM log showed no teammate link, and the Village had nothing to build a PM-triangle case on.

tips_feedback.tip: After a failed Katana, assume protection or innate Defense: kill or block the protector, or hang the survivor, rather than retrying blindly.
tips_feedback.why: Erin survived the N4 Katana because Heidi protected her, and Heidi died that morning, so the N5 retry on Erin, the Lookout, was the right follow-up and succeeded.

tips_feedback.tip: Give the Katana to a low-value member with a cover story ready, and move it the same night a Lookout or Tracker names the holder.
tips_feedback.why: I was a Grunt holding the Katana with only a Vanilla claim and no cover story; Carol's Seer pair named me, and the Village hanged me on the vote history that followed.

tips_feedback.tip: Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty. But first do the vote math in night chat.
tips_feedback.why: I voted Yes on Bob's Day 3 nomination, Innocent at his trial, and No on his Day 4 nomination, a mismatch the Village used as the case against me on Days 5 and 6.

lessons.tip: Do the trial vote math before deciding to bus a teammate. On Mallory’s trial, two Yakuza Innocent votes would have reduced the Guilty total from 7 of 10 to 5 of 10—exactly half, not a majority. The teammate was still savable.

A fake investigative claim must fit its mechanical footprint as well as its result. Framing someone can explain an Evil alignment result, but it cannot explain why a claimed Sheriff check produced no visit for the Lookout to see.

Before spending a swap token, map every action it redirects—including the Katana attack and investigators’ targets—and coordinate the intended result with the team. Saving a token is better than causing an unpredictable redirection.

Plan for the actual faction win condition, not parity. If the last Yakuza reaches a 1-versus-2 endgame against coordinated Village players, survival alone is not a path to victory; preserve cover and build a credible way to remove every opponent.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim only a role whose token count matches yours and that no living holder, Lookout or Tracker can contradict.
tips_feedback.why: This was exactly the risk in Mallory’s Sheriff claim: Erin’s Lookout report showed no visit to Ivan by Mallory, and Alice’s Tracker results supported the surrounding visit log. The possible Roleplayer explanation did not erase the contradiction.

tips_feedback.tip: Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty, but first do the vote math; if Innocent votes can save them, defend them.
tips_feedback.why: The vote-math caveat mattered: Bob and Judy both voted Guilty on Mallory, though switching both to Innocent would have left only 5 Guilty votes out of 10, so the execution would not have passed. Mallory was not doomed by the ballot.

tips_feedback.tip: Vigilantes should shoot only on a mechanical lead, not a soft read, and should use Basic shots.
tips_feedback.why: Frank spent all three tokens on a Strong shot at Heidi based on vote history and suspicion, killing a Good Medic. A mechanical lead and a Basic shot would have avoided wasting the extra tokens.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, check who voted No on their nomination or Innocent when it could have saved them.
tips_feedback.why: Judy’s Innocent vote on Bob was a genuine team-protection clue after Bob flipped Fabricator, and it helped focus the final case on the last Yakuza. Her No vote on Mallory’s nomination was less conclusive by itself, since she later voted Guilty.

summary: Village won, but narrowly and largely through Yakuza self-destruction. On Day 2 Mallory (Smuggler, holding the Katana) fake-claimed Sheriff with 'Ivan: Evil' to piggyback on Bob's frame. Erin had happened to watch Ivan, so her Lookout result showed no Mallory visit, Alice's track corroborated it, and Mallory was hanged 7-3. Bob's frame was wasted, because the real Sheriff checked Dave. Bob then fake-claimed Medic while the real Medic, Heidi, was alive. He survived a Day 3 trial 0-8 because his N1 visit to Ivan was corroborated and nobody had a 'mechanical contradiction'. On Day 4 he publicly typed 'Yakuza Fabricator' and was hanged 4-3. Meanwhile the Village made serious errors. They fixated on Carol's and Heidi's Innocent votes on Mallory; those votes were meaningless, since Guilty already had 7 votes. Frank spent all 3 Vigilante tokens killing Heidi (Good Medic) on that soft read. That same night Heidi's free Standard protection saved Erin. On Day 5 Carol, the real Seer, correctly pointed at Judy: her Heidi/Judy pair matched, so Judy was either Good or the Katana holder. Carol's earlier flip-flops (nominating Mallory, then voting Innocent; a weak Alice nomination) made her the hang target instead. Judy (Grunt, Katana) cast the deciding third Guilty vote on Carol and killed Erin that night. At 3 alive, Grace reasoned that Judy was the only remaining possible Katana holder, and Frank joined her to hang Judy.

lessons.tip: Don't fake-claim an investigator result whose action would have needed a visit to a player that a Lookout or Tracker may have watched. Pairing a frame with a fake Sheriff check on the same target draws attention to that target. If you must fake a check, fake one on a target nobody is likely to be watching, or claim a non-visiting role.
lessons.evidence: Mallory claimed she checked Ivan N1. Erin had watched Ivan and saw only Alice and Bob visit, Alice corroborated it, and Mallory was nominated 8-2 and hanged 7-3 on that contradiction alone.

lessons.tip: Before fake-claiming a protective role, consider that the real holder may be alive and will counterclaim. Once your cover survives a trial, keep every later message strictly in character; one slip naming your faction or role is fatal.
lessons.evidence: Bob's Medic claim was counterclaimed by the real Medic Heidi but survived a 0-8 trial on Day 3. On Day 4 he wrote 'Bob here, Yakuza Fabricator' and was hanged 4-3 the same day.

lessons.tip: Never shoot on vote history or an unresolved counterclaim. If you do shoot on a lead, use a Basic shot rather than all your tokens. Killing a protector also strips protection from whoever they would have saved.
lessons.evidence: Frank spent all 3 tokens on a Strong shot at Heidi because of her Innocent vote on Mallory and the Medic counterclaim. Heidi was the Good Medic, and that same night her Standard protection saved Erin from the Katana. Frank was left with no shots for the endgame.

lessons.tip: A Seer 'same alignment' pair that includes a confirmed-Good player means the other player is Good or was holding the Katana that night. Combine this with elimination (a confirmed Vigilante, players who survived a Katana attack, flips) to narrow down the holder, rather than dismissing Seer pairs as 'untestable'.
lessons.evidence: Carol's N4 pair Heidi/Judy matched. Frank was confirmed by his shot and Erin had been attacked, which left Judy, Grace or Carol. The Village dismissed the pair and hanged Carol, the real Seer. Judy, the Katana holder, then killed Erin and nearly won.

lessons.tip: Judge votes on a flipped Yakuza by whether they could have changed the outcome. Innocent votes against a large Guilty majority prove little. A No vote on the nomination, or a Guilty vote cast once the hang was certain, is the more telling pattern. Don't let an opponent drive the agenda by repeating someone else's vote history.
lessons.evidence: Bob repeatedly hammered Carol's and Heidi's futile Innocent votes on Mallory, whose trial was already 7-3. Both were Good, and both were later killed by the Village. Judy had voted No on Mallory's nomination and Guilty at trial; that pattern was only acted on by Grace on Day 6.

lessons.tip: If you nominate someone, vote consistently with your own case. Don't nominate a corroborated investigator on a theory you can't back up. Flip-flops and weak nominations make a real power role look like a scum leader.
lessons.evidence: Carol nominated Mallory, then voted Innocent, and later nominated Alice, the corroborated Tracker, over a Katana-holder theory. On Day 5 Erin, Frank and Judy cited exactly these moves to hang her 3-2.

lessons.tip: Don't send nightly target plans by private message on a day the Yakuza are hunting investigators. Everyone sees that the PM was sent, and that marks you as an investigator worth killing.
lessons.evidence: Alice PM'd Erin her tracking plan at the end of Day 3. In night chat Bob cited 'who just PM'd Erin' when choosing Alice, and the Katana killed her that night.

lessons.tip: In the final three, list who is confirmed Good (by mechanical results or your own role) and treat everyone else as a possible Katana holder. Don't let the last Yakuza reframe the vote as 'votes only, no mechanics'.
lessons.evidence: On Day 6 Grace reasoned: Frank was confirmed by his Vigilante shot, she knew she was Good, and Erin had died to the Katana, so Judy had to be the holder. Frank agreed, and they hanged Judy 2-1 despite her Jester/Executioner deflection.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results.
tips_feedback.why: The Village hanged Mallory on a clear mechanical contradiction: a claimed Sheriff check with no visit behind it. The same standard also cut the other way: it got Bob, a Yakuza, acquitted 0-8 on Day 3, though it also kept the Village from hanging Heidi on a counterclaim.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them.
tips_feedback.why: Players applied it loosely to Carol's and Heidi's Innocent votes, which could not have saved Mallory. Bob exploited this, which led to Frank shooting Heidi and contributed to Carol's hanging. Judy's actual No on the nomination was used correctly only on Day 6.

tips_feedback.tip: Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty. But first do the vote math in night chat.
tips_feedback.why: Bob voted Yes and Guilty on Mallory and gained enough credibility to survive the Medic counterclaim. Judy's futile No on Mallory's nomination was later the core of Grace's case against her.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting.
tips_feedback.why: Carol shows the cost of ignoring it. Her nominate-then-Innocent on Mallory became the recurring case against her and got the Good Seer hanged on Day 5.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim only a role whose token count matches yours and that no living holder, Lookout or Tracker can contradict.
tips_feedback.why: Mallory and Bob both broke it. Mallory's fake Sheriff check was contradicted by Erin's Lookout watch and she was hanged. Bob's Medic claim was counterclaimed by the real Medic, which kept him under suspicion until his slip.

issues.description: Day 4: Bob (Yakuza Fabricator) posted the public message 'Bob here, Yakuza Fabricator with no Medic claim changed.' He then sent feedback saying he never sent it and calling it a possible transcription error. Either the harness attributed or garbled a message, or the model leaked its real role and then disowned it. The log cannot tell which. This one message decided Bob's nomination and hanging. It should be checked against the raw model output: a harness attribution bug would be serious, and a player leak would be serious player confusion.
Day 4: Erin's first answer nominated Mallory, who was already dead. The harness rejected it (player_error) and she retried.
Day 5: Grace's answer was cut off at the output length limit (finish_reason length), giving unparsable JSON and a retry. The response format or token budget may be too tight for long turns.

Night 3 Yakuza chat: Judy first said Heidi's Standard protection would stop the Standard Katana, which is correct. She then said 'Heidi's Standard protection is possible but can't stop Standard', which contradicts R3: an attack must be strictly higher than Defense to kill.
Day 3: Frank said 'N1 self-protection would not create a visit'. Under R6, a Medic, who can target others, shows as visiting themself when self-protecting. Heidi correctly cited R6 earlier.
Day 1: several players (Judy, Bob, Dave, Alice) asked for Night 1 results or actions during Day 1, before any night had happened. Frank and Heidi had to point out that the game starts on Day 1.

Day 5: Grace questioned Erin's Night 4 survival, assuming Heidi had no tokens and so could not protect. The Medic's Standard protection of another player is free, so the survival was legitimate. Others corrected her.

Erin noted it is unclear whether a Lookout may watch themself. R6 allows self-targeting by default, and the Lookout text ('not counting your own visit') suggests it is possible, but there is no explicit statement. A clarifying line would help.
